A disparity is a significant, noticeable difference or gap between two or more things — especially when that difference involves an imbalance or inequality that feels unfair, surprising, or troubling.

The plural form is disparities.

This is the most important thing to understand. In English, we have many words for "difference" — but they are not all the same.

When you say two things are different, you are simply saying they are not identical. That's neutral. Your shirt and my shirt are different colors. That's just a fact, with no judgment attached.

But when you use the word disparity, you are saying something stronger. You are pointing to a difference that is large enough to be concerning, often one that should not exist, or one that reveals an injustice or imbalance. It's a difference that demands attention.

Think of it this way: all disparities are differences, but not all differences are disparities.

Disparity almost always carries an unspoken expectation that the two things being compared should be more similar or more equal than they actually are.

For example, if two employees do the exact same job, with the same experience, same skills, and same performance — but one earns significantly more than the other — that gap in pay is a disparity. It's not just a difference. It's an unjustified, unequal difference.

This is the quiet but powerful emotion behind the word: there is a gap where there should not be one, or the gap is far bigger than it should be.

Here are clear examples across different areas of life, so you can see how widely the word is used:

Health:
"There is a serious disparity in access to medical care between rich and poor neighborhoods. People in wealthy areas can see a doctor easily, while people in poor areas often cannot."

Education:
"Researchers found large disparities in the quality of schools across the country. Children in some regions received an excellent education, while children in others were left far behind."

Income:
"The income disparity between the company's top executives and its lowest-paid workers has grown dramatically over the past decade."

Gender:
"Despite years of progress, a wage disparity between men and women still exists in many industries."

Performance / Results:
"There was a striking disparity between the team's performance at home and away — they won almost every home game but lost nearly every away game."

Disparity is not an emotionally neutral word. When someone uses it, they are usually implying one or more of the following:

  • The gap is large — not a minor or trivial difference.
  • The gap is unjust — it should not exist, or it exists because of an unfair system.
  • The gap is worth paying attention to — it has real consequences for real people.
  • The gap needs to be addressed or fixed.

This is why you will constantly see this word in journalism, academic writing, policy discussions, social justice conversations, and research. It is the word people reach for when they want to highlight an inequality that has weight and meaning.
How Disparity Is Different from Similar Words

Disparity vs. Discrepancy
A discrepancy usually refers to an inconsistency or mismatch in data, records, or facts — something that doesn't add up. Example: "There was a discrepancy between what the witness said and what the security footage showed." A disparity, on the other hand, is about inequality in scale, amount, quality, or opportunity between groups or things.

Disparity vs. Gap
A gap is more general and neutral — it can even be physical (a gap between two teeth). A disparity is specifically about inequality and imbalance, and it almost always has a social, economic, or moral dimension.

Disparity vs. Inequality
These are very close. Inequality directly states that things are not equal. Disparity emphasizes the size and visibility of that inequality — the fact that the difference is large enough to stand out and demand notice.
Common Ways It Appears in Sentences

You will most often see disparity used in these patterns:

  • "A disparity between X and Y" — "There is a glaring disparity between the promises made and the results delivered."
  • "Disparity in X" — "Researchers are studying disparities in healthcare outcomes."
  • "[Adjective] disparity" — "A wide disparity," "a stark disparity," "a significant disparity," "a growing disparity," "a racial/gender/income/wealth disparity."
  • "Address / close / narrow / reduce the disparity" — These are common action verbs used with the word, because disparity is something people try to fix.

If you had to boil it all down: a disparity is a large, often unjust gap between two things that are supposed to be more equal — and the word is a signal that this gap is serious, visible, and worth doing something about.
